blocks.text:
Design an LRU (Least Recently Used) Cache with a fixed capacity, supporting get and put operations that both run in O(1) time. When the cache is full and a new key needs to be inserted, the least recently used entry must be evicted first.

  • Actors: application code reading and writing cached values, a monitoring system observing evictions.
  • Scope: a single, in-process cache instance with a fixed maximum capacity.
  • Goal: guarantee O(1) get and put, and guarantee the evicted entry is always the true least recently used one.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: every get or put must run in constant time, and eviction must always remove the entry that was used longest ago. Everything else in the design serves that guarantee.

items: get(key) shall return the value for a key if present, and mark that key as most recently used.
put(key, value) shall insert or update a key, and mark it as most recently used.
When put() is called on a full cache with a new key, the least recently used entry shall be evicted first.
The system shall support registering listeners that are notified whenever an entry is evicted.
The system shall report its current size at any time.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: speed, bounded memory, correctness and extensibility

items: Speed: both get() and put() must run in O(1) time, regardless of how many entries the cache holds.
Bounded memory: the cache must never hold more entries than its configured capacity.
Correctness: the evicted entry must always be the genuinely least recently used one, never an approximation.
Extensibility: it should be possible to swap in a different eviction rule (e.g. least frequently used) without rewriting the cache’s core get/put logic.
Thread Safety: concurrent get and put calls from different threads must never corrupt the internal linked list.
Should the cache be thread-safe, or is it used from a single thread only? Assume thread safety is required unless stated otherwise.
What should get() return for a missing key, null/None, or should it throw?
Is there a maximum key or value size to worry about, or can we assume both fit comfortably in memory?
Should updating an existing key’s value also count as "using" it, moving it to most recently used?
Do we need to support cache-wide operations like clear() or iterating all entries in usage order?
Capacity is fixed at construction time and does not change afterward.
A get() on a missing key returns null (Java), None (Python), or an empty optional (C++), it does not throw.
Updating an existing key via put() counts as a use, and moves that key to most recently used, matching the standard interview specification.
The cache is a single in-process instance, not distributed across machines.
Persistence is out of scope for the core cache; a database design is still covered separately for eviction auditing.

metadata.alt: LRUCache combining a HashMap for O(1) lookup, a doubly linked list for usage order, and a listener list for eviction notifications

items: Node: one doubly linked list node holding a key, a value, and pointers to its neighbors.
HashMap (key to Node): gives O(1) lookup straight to the node for any key.
Doubly linked list: keeps every node ordered by recency, most recently used at the head, least at the tail.
CacheEvictionListener: anything that wants to react when an entry is evicted.
LRUCache: the facade tying the HashMap, linked list, and listeners together behind a simple get/put interface.

metadata.alt: LRUCache composing a HashMap and a doubly linked list bounded by head and tail sentinels

items: Composition: LRUCache composes its HashMap and its head/tail sentinel nodes, neither makes sense without the cache instance that owns them.
Association: LRUCache is associated with zero or more CacheEvictionListener instances, added independently of the cache’s own lifecycle.
Aggregation: each HashMap entry points to a Node that also lives in the doubly linked list, the same node is shared by both structures at once.
Realization: PrintEvictionListener realizes CacheEvictionListener; LeastRecentlyUsedStrategy realizes EvictionStrategy.

metadata.alt: LRUCache tying together Node, CacheEvictionListener and EvictionStrategy

blocks.text: Notice that LRUCache exposes only get() and put() publicly, everything else (addToFront, remove, moveToFront, evictLeastRecentlyUsed) is private. This is the Facade pattern in action, covered next.
Three patterns make this design clean and genuinely extensible, not just a working solution.

metadata.alt: Client code only ever calling get and put, with the HashMap lookups and linked list pointer surgery hidden behind them

blocks.text: Why needed: correctly maintaining a HashMap and a doubly linked list in sync is genuinely fiddly, exposing that complexity to callers invites bugs. Why best: LRUCache presents exactly two public methods, get and put, callers never need to know a linked list is involved at all. What it solves: keeps the tricky pointer manipulation entirely internal and testable in one place.

metadata.alt: LRUCache depending on an EvictionStrategy interface, with LeastRecentlyUsedStrategy and a future LeastFrequentlyUsedStrategy both fitting behind it

blocks.text: Why needed: "least recently used" is one specific eviction rule among several real caches actually use (LFU, FIFO, random). Why best: framing eviction as a swappable EvictionStrategy means a future LFU cache reuses the exact same LRUCache scaffolding. What it solves: decouples "which entry to evict" from the cache’s core get/put mechanics.

metadata.alt: LRUCache notifying every registered CacheEvictionListener whenever an entry is evicted

blocks.text: Why needed: production systems often want to react to evictions, recording metrics, logging, or triggering a write-back to slower storage, without the cache itself knowing any of that. Why best: new listener types can be added freely without ever touching LRUCache’s own code. What it solves: keeps eviction notification fully decoupled from eviction mechanics.

items: LRUCache: responsibility is exposing get/put in O(1) while enforcing capacity. Attributes: capacity, map, head, tail, listeners. Methods: get(), put(), addEvictionListener(), size(), and private addToFront()/remove()/moveToFront()/evictLeastRecentlyUsed().
Node: responsibility is holding one key-value pair plus its position in the usage order. Attributes: key, value, prev, next. No methods, purely a data holder.
PrintEvictionListener: responsibility is a simple concrete reaction to an eviction (printing it). Methods: onEvict(key, value).

metadata.alt: EvictionStrategy and CacheEvictionListener as the two extension points, each with one concrete implementation shown

blocks.text: EvictionStrategy isolates the eviction rule itself, letting LRU be swapped for LFU or another policy. CacheEvictionListener isolates reactions to an eviction, letting metrics, logging, or write-back logic be added without ever touching the cache’s core.
Three workflows matter most: a successful get, a put that has room to spare, and a put that must evict first.

metadata.alt: get(1) finding the node in the HashMap, then moving it to the front of the linked list before returning its value

blocks.text: A hit does two things: it returns the value, and it moves that node to the front of the list, since it was just used.

metadata.alt: put(3, "C") inserting a new node directly since the cache still has room

blocks.text: When the cache is below capacity, a new key is simply added to both the HashMap and the front of the linked list, no eviction needed.

metadata.alt: put(3, "C") on a full cache, evicting the node at the tail before inserting the new one

blocks.text: When the cache is at capacity, the node at tail.prev, the true least recently used entry, is removed first, notifying any eviction listeners, before the new entry is added.

metadata.alt: The shared shape of both get and put: look up the key, then branch on whether it was found

items: Happy path, get hit: HashMap lookup succeeds, node is moved to the front, value is returned.
Happy path, put update: key already exists, its value is updated in place and the node is moved to the front.
Happy path, put insert with eviction: key is new, cache is full, the tail.prev node is evicted, then the new node is added at the front.
Miss scenario: get() on a key that was never inserted, or was already evicted, simply returns null/None/nullopt, no exception.
get(K key): returns the value for key, or null/None/nullopt if absent, and marks the key as most recently used.
put(K key, V value): inserts or updates a key, evicting the least recently used entry first if the cache is full.
addEvictionListener(CacheEvictionListener): registers a listener to be notified on every future eviction.
size(): returns the current number of entries in the cache.

metadata.alt: Constructing the cache with an invalid, non-positive capacity failing fast rather than allowing an unusable cache to exist

items: Invalid input: constructing an LRUCache with a zero or negative capacity throws immediately, an unusable cache should never be allowed to exist.
Resource unavailable: not applicable in the in-memory version, but a distributed variant backed by a remote store would need to handle store timeouts here.
Business-rule violation: attempting to bypass the capacity check (inserting without checking size first) is impossible by construction, put() always checks before inserting.
System failure: a broken eviction listener throwing an exception should be caught and logged per-listener, not allowed to abort the eviction itself.

metadata.alt: A get call and a put call from different threads both needing to safely mutate the same shared linked list pointers

blocks.text: get() and put() both mutate the linked list (moveToFront, addToFront, remove), if two threads run these concurrently without protection, pointers can be corrupted, producing a broken list or a lost node entirely. Both methods must be synchronized around the same lock (a synchronized block in Java, a threading.Lock in Python, a std::mutex in C++) so no two pointer mutations can ever interleave.

items: Swapping LRU for LFU (least frequently used) would mean introducing an EvictionStrategy implementation that tracks access counts instead of recency, without changing LRUCache’s get/put contract.
Adding TTL (time-to-live) expiry would mean checking a stored expiry timestamp inside get(), evicting expired entries lazily on access.
Adding a write-back listener that persists evicted entries to disk or a database is a pure CacheEvictionListener implementation, no core changes needed.
Future work: sharding the cache across multiple instances for higher throughput would sit as a routing layer above LRUCache, not a change to it.
Single Responsibility: Node only holds data, LRUCache only manages capacity and ordering, listeners only react to evictions.
Open/Closed: new eviction strategies and listener types can be added without modifying LRUCache’s public interface.
Liskov Substitution: any CacheEvictionListener implementation can be registered without LRUCache needing to know which one it is.
Interface Segregation: CacheEvictionListener and EvictionStrategy are each a single narrow method, no unnecessary methods to implement.
Dependency Inversion: LRUCache depends on the CacheEvictionListener interface, never on a specific concrete listener.
Capacity of 1: every put() on a new key immediately evicts the single existing entry.
Calling get() on an empty cache: must return null/None/nullopt cleanly, not throw.
Calling put() repeatedly on the exact same key: value updates in place, size never grows past 1 entry for that key.
Evicting while a listener is registered that itself calls back into the cache: must not cause reentrant corruption of the linked list.
get(): O(1), a HashMap lookup plus a constant number of pointer updates.
put(): O(1) amortized, a HashMap lookup/insert plus a constant number of pointer updates, even when eviction is triggered.
Space: O(capacity), exactly one HashMap entry and one linked list node per cached key, regardless of how many get/put calls have been made.

metadata.alt: CACHE_INSTANCE tracking configured CACHE_ENTRY rows and an EVICTION_LOG history for auditing

blocks.text: The live cache itself is purely in-memory, but a production deployment still benefits from a lightweight audit trail. CACHE_INSTANCE stores configuration per named cache, CACHE_ENTRY optionally mirrors last-accessed metadata for monitoring, and EVICTION_LOG records every eviction for later analysis of hit/miss and eviction patterns.

items: How would you extend this to a distributed LRU cache shared across multiple servers?
How would you add TTL-based expiry on top of the existing recency-based eviction?
How would you make the cache safely support high-concurrency workloads without a single global lock becoming a bottleneck?
How would you test that eviction always picks the true least recently used entry, especially under concurrent access?

blocks.text: Complete, self-contained, directly runnable file (every class above combined into one file per language, exactly as you would actually copy, compile and run it):

codes.java:
src/
  main/
    java/
      lrucache/
        Node.java
        CacheEvictionListener.java
        PrintEvictionListener.java
        LRUCache.java
        Main.java

items: Why use dummy head and tail sentinel nodes instead of tracking the real head/tail pointers directly? Sentinels remove every null check from addToFront/remove, every real node always has a genuine prev and next to update, which is what makes the pointer surgery O(1) and bug-free.

Why does put() on an existing key still call moveToFront() even though the key was not "read"? Because the specification defines both get and put as a "use" of the key, updating a value is itself an access.

What is the actual difference between this and a plain HashMap with a separate list of keys sorted by recency? Sorting a list on every access would be O(n log n) or worse, the doubly linked list gets the same recency ordering in O(1) per operation.

A simpler alternative uses Java’s LinkedHashMap with access-order mode, which gives LRU behavior in a few lines, at the cost of hiding the actual mechanics this problem is meant to test understanding of.
Using a single array with periodic compaction instead of a linked list would avoid pointer overhead, but moving an accessed element to the front would cost O(n), breaking the O(1) requirement.

A more advanced production cache might use a "clock" or "second-chance" approximation instead of exact LRU ordering, trading a small amount of eviction accuracy for reduced per-access overhead at very large scale.
Guard every linked list mutation with a single lock (or a concurrent-safe structure) to prevent the exact race condition described in section 16.
Expose cache hit/miss counters alongside the eviction listener hook, so cache effectiveness can be monitored in production, not just its correctness.
Consider capacity in terms of memory footprint, not just entry count, if values vary wildly in size, a fixed entry-count capacity can still let memory usage spike unexpectedly.
Log evictions sparingly in high-throughput systems, a listener that prints on every eviction can itself become a performance bottleneck.
